extracted.intended_audience: general public, researchers, policymakers, campaigners and families interested in the Hillsborough disaster, stadium safety, and public-inquiry findings
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic summary of the Hillsborough disaster, the findings of inquiries and panels, subsequent legal and policy responses, and memorialisation. Covers safety standards for stadiums, conduct and accountability of police and public bodies, inquest procedures, and proposed legislative reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police must give orders to direct fans to empty areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure by the police to give the order to direct fans to empty areas of the stadium was described as 'a blunder of the first magnitude'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report criticises police for not issuing direction orders to move crowds into empty parts of the ground; effective crowd-direction orders are implied to be a necessary part of crowd control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means to calculate when enclosures reach capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no means for calculating when individual enclosures had reached capacity; a police officer ordinarily made a visual assessment before guiding fans to other pens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stadium control and policing should have objective means or procedures to assess enclosure occupancy rather than relying solely on informal visual assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid admitting people into pens that are over-full
rubrics_metrics.description: "By 2:52 pm when gate C was opened, pens 3 and 4 were over-full [...] to allow any more into those pens was likely to cause injuries; to allow in a large stream was courting disaster."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission controls must prevent large streams being allowed into pens already over capacity; opening entry points should consider pen occupancy to avoid causing crush injuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official capacity must account for crush barriers and perimeter gates
rubrics_metrics.description: The report noted that the official capacity of the central pens was 2,200, that the Health and Safety Executive found this should have been reduced to 1,693 due to crush barriers and perimeter gates, but actually an estimated 3,000 people were in the pens around 3:00 pm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity figures should be adjusted for installed infrastructure (crush barriers, gates) and enforced; failure to do so risks dangerous overcrowding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prioritise pitch sanctity over crowd safety
rubrics_metrics.description: "The anxiety to protect the sanctity of the pitch has caused insufficient attention to be paid to the risk of a crush due to overcrowding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Event and crowd-control decision-making must prioritise spectator safety over protecting playing surfaces or other property, including authorising rescue or entry onto the pitch when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior officers must show leadership expected of their rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior police officers' handling of the problems and their accounts 'did not show the qualities of leadership to be expected of their rank'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Command-level officers are expected to exercise decisive leadership, coordinate rescue efforts, give orders (e.g., to relieve pressure in tunnels) and take responsibility; lack of leadership is a critical failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing disaster causation to fan drunkenness without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord Taylor concluded most fans were 'not drunk, nor even the worse for drink' and that drunkenness was an exaggerated explanation used by police to rationalise loss of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials and investigators should base accounts of crowd behaviour on sound evidence and avoid overestimating alcohol as a causal factor in crowd incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency services response scrutiny and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Taylor concluded there had been no fault on the part of the emergency services (St John Ambulance, ambulance service and fire brigade) in responding to the disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating emergency response, inquiries should distinguish between on-scene rescue performance and wider command/coordination failures; emergency services should be assessed against expected operational standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and accountability of police witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior officers were described as 'defensive and evasive witnesses' who refused to accept responsibility; 'the quality of their evidence was in inverse proportion to their rank.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police witnesses, especially senior officers, are expected to give candid, accurate evidence; evasiveness and refusal to concede errors are serious criticisms in inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove perimeter and lateral fencing and move to all-seater stadia
rubrics_metrics.description: The Taylor Report had a deep impact on safety standards: perimeter and lateral fencing was removed and many top stadiums were converted to all-seated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical stadium design standards should eliminate barriers that create crush risk; transitioning to all-seater stadia was recommended to reduce standing-related overcrowding dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: League and regulatory requirements for seating
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose-built stadiums for Premier League and most Football League teams since the report are all-seater. In England and Wales all-seating is a requirement of the Premier League and of the Football League for clubs who have been present in the Championship for more than three seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: League membership and regulations can mandate seating policies to improve safety, with some tiered relaxations for lower leagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry remit limited to 'new evidence' (Stuart-Smith inquiry constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms of reference of Stuart-Smith's inquiry were limited to 'new evidence' — evidence which was not available or presented to previous inquiries, courts or authorities — thereby excluding some altered witness statements as inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of an inquiry's terms of reference materially affects what evidence is examinable; narrow remits can exclude potentially relevant material and are controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coroner's admissibility cut-off (3:15 pm determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stuart-Smith's report supported the coroner's assertion that evidence after 3:15 pm was inadmissible as 'by 3:15 pm the principal cause of death, that is, the crushing, was over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural cut-offs on admissibility of later evidence can limit scrutiny of emergency response and may be contested as to whether they exclude material issues for investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full public disclosure of relevant government and local information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hillsborough Independent Panel was tasked to investigate the disaster, oversee disclosure of documents and produce a report; it published 450,000 pages collated from 85 organisations and individuals and sought 'full public disclosure of relevant government and local information'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency and wide disclosure of documents are central to independent review processes; panels should collate and publish relevant records to enable public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of witness statements and prohibition on altering evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel found 164 witness statements had been altered; 116 were amended to remove or change negative comments about South Yorkshire Police.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering witness statements to sanitize or shift blame is a fundamental procedural abuse; inquiries and prosecutions depend on preserved, unaltered original accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate post-rescue medical handling (recovery position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing fans who were 'merely unconscious' on their backs rather than in the recovery position would have resulted in their deaths due to airway obstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First responders should apply established clinical procedures (e.g., recovery position) for unconscious but breathing casualties to prevent airway obstruction and improve survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigatory priorities for IPCC referrals
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPCC announced it would investigate failure to declare a major incident; failure to close the tunnel to the stands leading to overcrowded pens; changes made to statements of police officers; actions which misled Parliament and the media; shortcomings of previous investigations; and the role played by Norman Bettison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent police-oversight investigations should examine both operational decisions (incident declaration, venue control) and conduct (statement alterations, misleading officials and public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper participation of bereaved families at inquests (James Jones recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The report called for 'proper participation' of bereaved families at inquests — including publicly funded legal representation for bereaved families when public bodies are legally represented, controls on public bodies' legal spending, and changes to how public bodies approach inquests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquests should be fair and accessible: families must have effective representation and a balanced procedural environment when public bodies are legally represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charter for Families Bereaved through Public Tragedy — transparency commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: One of 25 'points of learning' was a 'Charter for Families Bereaved through Public Tragedy' — a series of commitments by public bodies to change, related to transparency and acting in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public bodies should adopt formal commitments (a charter) to ensure transparent, respectful treatment of bereaved families after public tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candour for police officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The report recommended a duty of candour for police officers — requiring them to cooperate fully with investigations into alleged criminal offences or misconduct, as undertaken by the IPCC or its successor body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police officers should be legally and ethically required to be truthful and to proactively cooperate with independent investigations into alleged wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Authority (Accountability) Bill / 'Hillsborough Law' proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed Public Authority (Accountability) Bill (informally 'Hillsborough Law') would include a legal duty of candour on public authorities and officials to be truthful and to proactively cooperate with official investigations and inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative mechanisms (a duty of candour) have been proposed to make public bodies legally accountable for truthful engagement with inquiries and investigations; the draft bill was appended to the Jones report though it has been contentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial decisions based on sufficiency of evidence and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Several charges were dropped or not pursued where prosecutors found insufficient evidence or that prosecution was not in the public interest (e.g., farrier not charged notwithstanding evidence, charges against Bettison dropped due to insufficient evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charging decisions should adhere to legal standards: sufficient admissible evidence and considerations of public interest guide whether to bring or continue prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standards on psychiatric injury for secondary victims (Alcock principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police held that claimants who watched the disaster on television or listened on radio were not 'proximal' and their claims for psychiatric injury were rejected; this was upheld in White v Chief Constable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil claims for psychiatric injury require proximity and other legal thresholds; courts have restricted secondary victim claims where the claimant lacked sufficient proximity to the traumatic event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness of withdrawing life-sustaining treatment (Airedale NHS Trust v Bland)
rubrics_metrics.description: Airedale N.H.S. Trust v Bland allowed the life-support machine of Tony Bland to be switched off; a landmark decision in English criminal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-authorised withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment in persistent vegetative states is subject to legal precedent and rigorous judicial consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorialisation practices and commemoration standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple permanent memorials and annual memorial ceremonies have been established (memorial at Anfield, rose gardens, plaques, clock indicating 3:06), with families deciding on how official memorials proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities and institutions should consult with victims' families when establishing memorials and commemorations; memorial practices can include plaques, gardens, annual services, and preservation of victim names and times.
